findings.summary: `pre_init_args` passes parameter definitions with default values to `__attrs_pre_init__` call instead of argument names
findings.evidence: In `_attrs_to_init_script` (src/attr/_make.py:2203, 2222, 2325), positional arguments with defaults or factories are appended to `args` as `arg = f"{arg_name}=attr_dict['{attr_name}'].default"` or `arg = f"{arg_name}=NOTHING"`. Previously, `pre_init_args` tracked only the bare `arg_name` for positional arguments (lines 2206, 2225, 2269 in base), while `args` tracked parameter definitions with default expressions. The diff removes `pre_init_args` tracking and sets `pre_init_args = args` at line 2325. Consequently, when `call_pre_init and pre_init_has_args` is true (line 2341), `self.__attrs_pre_init__({pre_init_args})` is generated with default value expressions as positional call arguments (e.g. `self.__attrs_pre_init__(x=attr_dict['x'].default)` or `self.__attrs_pre_init__(x=NOTHING)`), causing a syntax/runtime error or passing keyword assignments instead of variable names.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep `pre_init_args` tracking bare `arg_name` strings, or strip default expressions from positional arguments when constructing `pre_init_args` (similar to how `kw_only_args` splits on `=`).

findings.summary: Removing closure cell rewriting for property descriptors breaks zero-arg `super()` and `__class__` references in properties of slotted classes
findings.evidence:
In `_ClassBuilder._create_slots_class` (src/attr/_make.py:793-810), attrs iterates over items in `cls.__dict__` to rewrite closure cells referencing the original class (`self._cls`) to point to the newly recreated slotted clone class (`cls`). This allows methods using `__class__` or zero-argument `super()` to work with `slots=True`.

Removing the `isinstance(item, property)` branch causes `getattr(item, "__closure__", None)` to be called on property descriptors instead of `getattr(item.fget, "__closure__", None)`. Since `property` instances do not have a `__closure__` attribute (`item.fget` does), property getter functions that access `__class__` or call `super()` (such as `super().some_prop` or `return __class__`) will no longer have their closure cells updated to the slotted class clone.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore handling for `property` objects (checking `item.fget.__closure__`, or additionally `item.fset` and `item.fdel` if present) so property closure cells referencing the original class are properly rewritten.

findings_before_overseer.summary: Removing closure cell rewriting for property descriptors breaks zero-arg `super()` and `__class__` references in properties of slotted classes
findings_before_overseer.evidence:
In `_ClassBuilder._create_slots_class` (src/attr/_make.py:793-810), attrs iterates over items in `cls.__dict__` to rewrite closure cells referencing the original class (`self._cls`) to point to the newly recreated slotted clone class (`cls`). This allows methods using `__class__` or zero-argument `super()` to work with `slots=True`.

Removing the `isinstance(item, property)` branch causes `getattr(item, "__closure__", None)` to be called on property descriptors instead of `getattr(item.fget, "__closure__", None)`. Since `property` instances do not have a `__closure__` attribute (`item.fget` does), property getter functions that access `__class__` or call `super()` (such as `super().some_prop` or `return __class__`) will no longer have their closure cells updated to the slotted class clone.
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix: Restore handling for `property` objects (checking `item.fget.__closure__`, or additionally `item.fset` and `item.fdel` if present) so property closure cells referencing the original class are properly rewritten.

findings.summary: `disabled()` no longer restores previous state on exit, breaking nesting and re-enabling validators unexpectedly
findings.evidence: In src/attr/validators.py lines 83-87, `disabled()` previously captured the previous validator state (`prev = get_run_validators()`) and restored it in `finally:` (`set_run_validators(prev)`), as documented by `.. versionchanged:: 26.1.0 The contextmanager is nestable.` which was deleted in this diff. With the change to hardcode `set_run_validators(True)` on exit, nesting `disabled()` blocks or invoking `disabled()` when validators were already globally disabled (via `set_disabled(True)` / `set_run_validators(False)`) will silently re-enable validators upon exiting the inner/contained `with disabled():` block.
findings.suggested_fix:
Keep saving and restoring the previous state:
```python
prev = get_run_validators()
set_run_validators(False)
try:
    yield
finally:
    set_run_validators(prev)
```

prev = get_run_validators()

result.head: head

findings.summary: Replacing `__init__` with class-level `args = [msg]` breaks exception message and `args` on instantiation
findings.evidence:
In src/attr/exceptions.py lines 19-20:
`msg = "can't set attribute"`
`args: ClassVar[tuple[str]] = [msg]`

1) `args` is assigned a list (`[msg]`) instead of a tuple `(msg,)`, mismatching the type annotation `tuple[str]` and standard exception behavior where `e.args` is always a tuple.
2) More critically, removing `__init__` and defining `args` as a class attribute breaks instantiated exception formatting and args behavior in Python. When `BaseException` (and therefore `AttributeError`) is instantiated without arguments (e.g. `FrozenInstanceError()` or `raise FrozenInstanceError`), `BaseException.__init__()` initializes `self.args = ()` on the instance, overriding the class attribute `args`. Consequently:
- `str(FrozenError())` returns `""` instead of `"can't set attribute"`.
- `FrozenError().args` returns `()` instead of `("can't set attribute",)`.
- Printing/raising `FrozenError`, `FrozenInstanceError`, or `FrozenAttributeError` displays no error message.

Previously, `__init__` called `super().__init__(msg)`, ensuring `args` was set to `("can't set attribute",)` on the instance.
findings.suggested_fix:
Revert the simplification or keep `__init__` so `BaseException` is properly initialized with `msg`:

```python
class FrozenError(AttributeError):
    msg = "can't set attribute"

    def __init__(self, msg: str = msg):
        super().__init__(msg)
        self.msg = msg
```

findings_before_overseer.summary: Replacing `__init__` with class-level `args = [msg]` breaks exception message and `args` on instantiation
findings_before_overseer.evidence:
In src/attr/exceptions.py lines 19-20:
`msg = "can't set attribute"`
`args: ClassVar[tuple[str]] = [msg]`

1) `args` is assigned a list (`[msg]`) instead of a tuple `(msg,)`, mismatching the type annotation `tuple[str]` and standard exception behavior where `e.args` is always a tuple.
2) More critically, removing `__init__` and defining `args` as a class attribute breaks instantiated exception formatting and args behavior in Python. When `BaseException` (and therefore `AttributeError`) is instantiated without arguments (e.g. `FrozenInstanceError()` or `raise FrozenInstanceError`), `BaseException.__init__()` initializes `self.args = ()` on the instance, overriding the class attribute `args`. Consequently:
- `str(FrozenError())` returns `""` instead of `"can't set attribute"`.
- `FrozenError().args` returns `()` instead of `("can't set attribute",)`.
- Printing/raising `FrozenError`, `FrozenInstanceError`, or `FrozenAttributeError` displays no error message.

Previously, `__init__` called `super().__init__(msg)`, ensuring `args` was set to `("can't set attribute",)` on the instance.
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix:
Revert the simplification or keep `__init__` so `BaseException` is properly initialized with `msg`:

```python
class FrozenError(AttributeError):
    msg = "can't set attribute"

    def __init__(self, msg: str = msg):
        super().__init__(msg)
        self.msg = msg
```

findings.summary: Subclasses inherit `__attrs_types_resolved__ = True` from base classes, preventing `resolve_types` from running on subclasses
findings.evidence:
In src/attr/_funcs.py:380-392, `resolve_types` previously checked `getattr(cls, "__attrs_types_resolved__", None) != cls` and set `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__ = cls` (explicitly noting in the comment: 'We store the class we resolved so that subclasses know they haven't been resolved').

The new code changes this to `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__` and sets `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__ = True`. When a base class resolves its types, `Base.__attrs_types_resolved__` becomes `True`. When `resolve_types(Subclass)` is called on a subclass of `Base` that has not yet resolved its own types, attribute lookup `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__` inherits the `True` attribute from `Base`, causing `resolve_types` to skip resolving type hints for `Subclass`.
findings.suggested_fix: Revert to checking whether `getattr(cls, "__attrs_types_resolved__", None) != cls` and setting `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__ = cls`, or check `cls.__dict__.get("__attrs_types_resolved__", False)` to avoid inheriting the attribute from superclasses.

findings_before_overseer.evidence:
In src/attr/_funcs.py:380-392, `resolve_types` previously checked `getattr(cls, "__attrs_types_resolved__", None) != cls` and set `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__ = cls` (explicitly noting in the comment: 'We store the class we resolved so that subclasses know they haven't been resolved').

The new code changes this to `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__` and sets `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__ = True`. When a base class resolves its types, `Base.__attrs_types_resolved__` becomes `True`. When `resolve_types(Subclass)` is called on a subclass of `Base` that has not yet resolved its own types, attribute lookup `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__` inherits the `True` attribute from `Base`, causing `resolve_types` to skip resolving type hints for `Subclass`.
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix: Revert to checking whether `getattr(cls, "__attrs_types_resolved__", None) != cls` and setting `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__ = cls`, or check `cls.__dict__.get("__attrs_types_resolved__", False)` to avoid inheriting the attribute from superclasses.

findings.summary: Removing `ctx.params.update(kwargs)` in `Context.invoke` breaks parameter tracking for nested `forward()` calls.
findings.evidence: In src/click/core.py:703 (prior to removal), Context.invoke updated `ctx.params.update(kwargs)` when invoking another Command. Removing this line stops Context from tracking kwargs in `ctx.params` during command invocation, which breaks multi-level forwarding where a subsequent `forward()` call relies on `self.params` having been updated with the parameters of the invoked command. The corresponding Sphinx documentation notes ('versionchanged:: 8.0: All kwargs are tracked in params so they will be passed if forward is called at multiple levels') were also deleted rather than simplified.
findings.suggested_fix: Revert the removal of `ctx.params.update(kwargs)` in `Context.invoke` and restore the associated documentation.

findings_before_overseer.evidence: In src/click/core.py:703 (prior to removal), Context.invoke updated `ctx.params.update(kwargs)` when invoking another Command. findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix: Revert the removal of `ctx.params.update(kwargs)` in `Context.invoke` and restore the associated documentation.

findings.summary: Moving flag_value default assignment inside `if type is None` leaves `self.flag_value` as `None` when `type` is explicitly passed
findings.evidence: In `Option.__init__` (src/click/core.py:2614-2623), moving `flag_value = not self.default` inside `if is_flag and type is None:` causes `self.flag_value` to remain `None` whenever `is_flag=True`, `flag_value=None`, and `type` is explicitly provided (e.g., `type=bool`). As seen in `Option.add_to_parser` (src/click/core.py:2760-2766), single flag options without secondary options register their parser action with `const=self.flag_value`. With `self.flag_value` left as `None`, parsing `--flag` will store `None` instead of `True` (or `not self.default`).
findings.suggested_fix:
Compute `flag_value` whenever `is_flag and flag_value is None` before inspecting `type`, restoring:
```python
if is_flag and flag_value is None:
    flag_value = not self.default
```

findings_before_overseer.summary: Moving flag_value default assignment inside `if type is None` leaves `self.flag_value` as `None` when `type` is explicitly passed
findings_before_overseer.evidence: In `Option.__init__` (src/click/core.py:2614-2623), moving `flag_value = not self.default` inside `if is_flag and type is None:` causes `self.flag_value` to remain `None` whenever `is_flag=True`, `flag_value=None`, and `type` is explicitly provided (e.g., `type=bool`). As seen in `Option.add_to_parser` (src/click/core.py:2760-2766), single flag options without secondary options register their parser action with `const=self.flag_value`. With `self.flag_value` left as `None`, parsing `--flag` will store `None` instead of `True` (or `not self.default`).
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix:
Compute `flag_value` whenever `is_flag and flag_value is None` before inspecting `type`, restoring:
```python
if is_flag and flag_value is None:
    flag_value = not self.default
```

findings.summary: `Context.exit()` no longer closes registered cleanup callbacks and resources before raising `Exit`.
findings.evidence: In src/click/core.py:701-704, `self.close()` was removed from `Context.exit()`. `Context.exit()` previously invoked `self.close()` to ensure all callbacks registered with `call_on_close` and resources managed via `with_resource` / `ExitStack` are cleaned up prior to raising `Exit(code)`. Removing `self.close()` breaks cleanup when `ctx.exit()` is called outside a context manager scope or before the context block unwinds.
findings.suggested_fix:
Restore `self.close()` in `Context.exit()` to ensure registered teardown callbacks and resources are closed when exiting:
```python
    def exit(self, code: int = 0) -> t.NoReturn:
        """Exits the application with a given exit code."""
        self.close()
        raise Exit(code)
```

findings_before_overseer.summary: `Context.exit()` no longer closes registered cleanup callbacks and resources before raising `Exit`.
findings_before_overseer.evidence: In src/click/core.py:701-704, `self.close()` was removed from `Context.exit()`. `Context.exit()` previously invoked `self.close()` to ensure all callbacks registered with `call_on_close` and resources managed via `with_resource` / `ExitStack` are cleaned up prior to raising `Exit(code)`. Removing `self.close()` breaks cleanup when `ctx.exit()` is called outside a context manager scope or before the context block unwinds.
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix:
Restore `self.close()` in `Context.exit()` to ensure registered teardown callbacks and resources are closed when exiting:
```python
    def exit(self, code: int = 0) -> t.NoReturn:
        """Exits the application with a given exit code."""
        self.close()
        raise Exit(code)
```

findings.summary: Dropping the IPv4/IPv6/localhost handling changes how NO_PROXY works: IPv6 entries now produce invalid mount keys
findings.evidence: The new code turns every NO_PROXY entry into `all://*{hostname}` (o1, line 262). Before, IPv6 literals were bracketed (`all://[::1]`), and IPv4 and localhost entries were matched exactly. Now `NO_PROXY=::1` gives `all://*::1`. URLPattern (o3, line 397) passes this to `URL(pattern)`, where the colons get parsed as a host:port separator. URL creation then fails, so building a client fails whenever NO_PROXY contains an IPv6 address. At best the pattern just never matches. IPv4 and localhost entries also change from exact matches to wildcard suffix matches. The deleted comment said NO_PROXY can hold domains, IPv6, IPv4 and localhost, so this was intended behavior, not dead code. The task asked for a simplification, not a behavior change. No test covers IPv6 or CIDR entries in NO_PROXY (o2, o7, o8), which is why the suite still passes (check:pytest).
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the is_ipv4_hostname/is_ipv6_hostname branches, including bracketing for IPv6. Add test cases for NO_PROXY values like `::1`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and `192.168.0.0/16` to test_get_environment_proxies.

stages.notes: You reported nothing, but the diff deletes functional code, not just redundant code. The removed IPv4/IPv6/localhost branches in get_environment_proxies decided how NO_PROXY entries become URL patterns. When a diff labelled "simplify" deletes branches, ask whether the remaining path gives the same result for every input. Here it doesn't: an IPv6 entry like `::1` becomes the unbracketed `all://*::1`. Passing tests don't settle this, because no test covers IPv6 or CIDR NO_PROXY entries.

findings.summary: Removing the `"://"` check in `get_environment_proxies` breaks URL/scheme-qualified entries in `NO_PROXY`.
findings.evidence:
In `get_environment_proxies` (httpx/_utils.py:227-238), removing `if "://" in hostname: mounts[hostname] = None` breaks support for specifying scheme-prefixed URLs in `NO_PROXY` (e.g. `NO_PROXY=https://127.0.0.1` or `NO_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1`).

Previously, `hostname="https://127.0.0.1"` resulted in `mounts["https://127.0.0.1"] = None`. With this branch removed, `hostname="https://127.0.0.1"` falls through to the `else` branch and sets `mounts["all://*https://127.0.0.1"] = None`. When parsed by `URLPattern`, this invalid pattern prevents scheme-specific `NO_PROXY` bypasses from functioning correctly.

This behavior is explicitly documented in `docs/environment_variables.md` line 105 (`export NO_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1,python-httpx.org`) and tested in `tests/client/test_proxies.py` line 219 (`NO_PROXY: https://127.0.0.1`).
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the `if "://" in hostname: mounts[hostname] = None` check to support scheme-qualified entries in `NO_PROXY`.

findings_before_overseer.summary: Removing the `"://"` check in `get_environment_proxies` breaks URL/scheme-qualified entries in `NO_PROXY`.
findings_before_overseer.evidence:
In `get_environment_proxies` (httpx/_utils.py:227-238), removing `if "://" in hostname: mounts[hostname] = None` breaks support for specifying scheme-prefixed URLs in `NO_PROXY` (e.g. `NO_PROXY=https://127.0.0.1` or `NO_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1`).

Previously, `hostname="https://127.0.0.1"` resulted in `mounts["https://127.0.0.1"] = None`. With this branch removed, `hostname="https://127.0.0.1"` falls through to the `else` branch and sets `mounts["all://*https://127.0.0.1"] = None`. When parsed by `URLPattern`, this invalid pattern prevents scheme-specific `NO_PROXY` bypasses from functioning correctly.

This behavior is explicitly documented in `docs/environment_variables.md` line 105 (`export NO_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1,python-httpx.org`) and tested in `tests/client/test_proxies.py` line 219 (`NO_PROXY: https://127.0.0.1`).

findings.summary: Removing `_set_timeout` prevents manually constructed `Request` objects sent via `Client.send()` / `AsyncClient.send()` from inheriting the client's default timeout.
findings.evidence: In httpx/_client.py (lines 352-358), `build_request` sets the timeout extension on requests created through the client. However, users can also pass standalone `httpx.Request` instances directly to `client.send()` or `async_client.send()`. Previously, `_set_timeout(request)` in `send()` ensured that any request missing a timeout extension inherited `self.timeout`. Removing `_set_timeout` (diff lines -565 to -572, -923, -1672) causes requests sent via `client.send()` / `async_client.send()` that were not created with `build_request` to bypass the client's configured default timeout.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain `_set_timeout(request)` (or ensure timeout defaults are applied to `request.extensions` in `send()`) so that manually constructed `Request` instances sent via `client.send()` and `async_client.send()` respect the client's default timeout.

findings_before_overseer.summary: Removing `_set_timeout` prevents manually constructed `Request` objects sent via `Client.send()` / `AsyncClient.send()` from inheriting the client's default timeout.
findings_before_overseer.evidence: In httpx/_client.py (lines 352-358), `build_request` sets the timeout extension on requests created through the client. However, users can also pass standalone `httpx.Request` instances directly to `client.send()` or `async_client.send()`. Previously, `_set_timeout(request)` in `send()` ensured that any request missing a timeout extension inherited `self.timeout`. Removing `_set_timeout` (diff lines -565 to -572, -923, -1672) causes requests sent via `client.send()` / `async_client.send()` that were not created with `build_request` to bypass the client's configured default timeout.
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix: Retain `_set_timeout(request)` (or ensure timeout defaults are applied to `request.extensions` in `send()`) so that manually constructed `Request` instances sent via `client.send()` and `async_client.send()` respect the client's default timeout.

findings.summary: Removing `not isinstance(self._stream, SyncByteStream/AsyncByteStream)` causes `TypeError` on streams with `read()`/`aread()`
findings.evidence:
In `httpx/_types.py`, `SyncByteStream.read(self)` is implemented as `return b"".join([part for part in self])` (lines 120-134), consuming the entire stream and closing it. Similarly, `AsyncByteStream.aread(self)` in lines 136-150 consumes the entire async stream and closes it.

In `IteratorByteStream.__iter__` (httpx/_content.py lines 53-58) and `AsyncIteratorByteStream.__aiter__` (lines 78-83), removing `and not isinstance(self._stream, SyncByteStream)` and `and not isinstance(self._stream, AsyncByteStream)` causes any instance of `SyncByteStream` / `AsyncByteStream` passed as the underlying stream to execute the `read(self.CHUNK_SIZE)` / `aread(self.CHUNK_SIZE)` file-like branch.

Because `SyncByteStream.read()` takes no arguments and reads the ENTIRE stream at once (rather than taking a chunk size and returning partial chunks), calling `self._stream.read(self.CHUNK_SIZE)` will raise `TypeError: SyncByteStream.read() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given` (or if overridden, consume the entire stream at once in a single chunk instead of iterating over it).
findings.suggested_fix:
Retain the check ensuring the stream is not a `SyncByteStream` / `AsyncByteStream`:
```python
if hasattr(self._stream, "read") and not isinstance(
    self._stream, SyncByteStream
):
    ...
```
and
```python
if hasattr(self._stream, "aread") and not isinstance(
    self._stream, AsyncByteStream
):
    ...
```

findings.summary: Removing `keep_blank_values=True` in `parse_qs` causes empty query parameters in string inputs to be silently dropped.
findings.evidence: In httpx/_urls.py line 543, removing `keep_blank_values=True` causes `parse_qs` to use its default `keep_blank_values=False`. As a result, parsing query strings containing empty values (such as `"a="` or `"a=&b=1"`) silently drops those parameters (e.g., `httpx.QueryParams("a=")["a"]` will raise `KeyError` and `dict(httpx.QueryParams("a="))` will be `{}` instead of `{"a": ""}`). This causes inconsistent behavior between string initialization `QueryParams("a=")` and dict initialization `QueryParams({"a": ""})`.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore `keep_blank_values=True`: `self._dict = parse_qs(value, keep_blank_values=True)`

findings.summary: `nth_combination_with_replacement` incorrectly raises `ValueError` when `r > len(iterable)` and breaks empty combinations when `n == 0, r == 0`
findings.evidence:
In more_itertools/more.py:4276, `if (r < 0) or (r > n): raise ValueError` was introduced. Unlike `combinations(iterable, r)` without replacement (where choosing r > n items is impossible), `combinations_with_replacement(iterable, r)` allows r to be arbitrarily large as long as n > 0 (e.g. `list(combinations_with_replacement([0, 1], 3))` has 4 combinations of length 3 from 2 elements).

Calling `nth_combination_with_replacement([0, 1], 3, 0)` previously returned `(0, 0, 0)`, which matches `list(combinations_with_replacement([0, 1], 3))[0]`. With this change, it now raises `ValueError` whenever `r > len(iterable)`, violating the documented contract "Equivalent to list(combinations_with_replacement(iterable, r))[index]".

Furthermore, when n == 0 and r == 0, `combinations_with_replacement([], 0)` yields one 0-length combination `()`. Previously `nth_combination_with_replacement([], 0, 0)` handled this via `c = comb(n + r - 1, r) if n else 0 if r else 1` (giving c=1). With `c = comb(-1, 0)` (which in Python's math.comb evaluates to 0), `index=0` causes `IndexError` instead of returning `()`.
findings.suggested_fix: Revert the check `(r > n)` (or keep only `if r < 0: raise ValueError`), update docstring, and restore the calculation of `c` for `n == 0` (e.g., `c = comb(n + r - 1, r) if n else 0 if r else 1`).

trigger_reasons: 1 major/blocker finding(s) from the primary reviewer

findings_before_overseer.summary: `nth_combination_with_replacement` incorrectly raises `ValueError` when `r > len(iterable)` and breaks empty combinations when `n == 0, r == 0`
findings_before_overseer.evidence:
In more_itertools/more.py:4276, `if (r < 0) or (r > n): raise ValueError` was introduced. Unlike `combinations(iterable, r)` without replacement (where choosing r > n items is impossible), `combinations_with_replacement(iterable, r)` allows r to be arbitrarily large as long as n > 0 (e.g. `list(combinations_with_replacement([0, 1], 3))` has 4 combinations of length 3 from 2 elements).

Calling `nth_combination_with_replacement([0, 1], 3, 0)` previously returned `(0, 0, 0)`, which matches `list(combinations_with_replacement([0, 1], 3))[0]`. With this change, it now raises `ValueError` whenever `r > len(iterable)`, violating the documented contract "Equivalent to list(combinations_with_replacement(iterable, r))[index]".

Furthermore, when n == 0 and r == 0, `combinations_with_replacement([], 0)` yields one 0-length combination `()`. Previously `nth_combination_with_replacement([], 0, 0)` handled this via `c = comb(n + r - 1, r) if n else 0 if r else 1` (giving c=1). With `c = comb(-1, 0)` (which in Python's math.comb evaluates to 0), `index=0` causes `IndexError` instead of returning `()`.
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix: Revert the check `(r > n)` (or keep only `if r < 0: raise ValueError`), update docstring, and restore the calculation of `c` for `n == 0` (e.g., `c = comb(n + r - 1, r) if n else 0 if r else 1`).

stages.notes: The diff changes only the docstring; none of the code changes. I read the implementation (ref:o1). When the items can't be sorted, it groups equal items under their first index and cycles through each group when building output. That matches the new docstring's description. Removing the two skipped doctests drops no test coverage. Two things are worth knowing, neither a defect. First, the task asks to simplify the implementation, but the change is documentation only. Second, the new wording has a small grammar slip ("forming equivalent group"). Having no findings is reasonable here.

findings.summary: exactly_n now raises ValueError when n <= -2. Before this change it returned False.
findings.evidence: The old code had an explicit `if n < 0: return False` branch. The new one-liner passes `n + 1` as the stop argument to `islice` [ref:o2]. When n <= -2, that stop is negative, and `itertools.islice` raises `ValueError: Stop argument for islice() must be None or an integer: 0 <= x <= sys.maxsize`. The only negative-n test is `exactly_n([True], -1)` [ref:o1]. With n = -1 the stop is 0, which is still valid, so the suite passes [ref:check:pytest] even though the behavior changed for every smaller n.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the guard: `if n < 0: return False` before the one-liner, or use `n >= 0 and ilen(islice(filter(predicate, iterable), n + 1)) == n`. Add a test for e.g. n = -2.

findings.summary: Replacing `getattr(..., None)` with `hasattr` mishandles objects with `__reversed__ = None`
findings.evidence: In more_itertools/more.py:286, `if getattr(iterable, '__reversed__', None):` was replaced with `if hasattr(iterable, '__reversed__'):`. In Python's data model, a class can explicitly opt out of reverse iteration or disable `__reversed__` by setting `__reversed__ = None` (e.g., dict keys/values/views in older Python or custom mappings/iterables). `hasattr(iterable, '__reversed__')` evaluates to `True` when `__reversed__` is set to `None`, leading to `reversed(iterable)` raising a `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable` instead of falling through to `deque(iterable, maxlen=1)[-1]`.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep `if getattr(iterable, '__reversed__', None):` or check `callable(getattr(iterable, '__reversed__', None))` to ensure `__reversed__` is not `None`.

findings.summary: `iterate` no longer terminates when `func` raises `StopIteration`
findings.evidence: In more_itertools/more.py:475-480, `iterate(func, start)` previously caught `StopIteration` raised by `func(start)` and broke the loop to cleanly terminate iteration. findings.suggested_fix: Keep the `try...except StopIteration: break` handling around `func(start)` so callers can terminate the iteration by raising `StopIteration` from `func`.

findings_before_overseer.evidence: In more_itertools/more.py:475-480, `iterate(func, start)` previously caught `StopIteration` raised by `func(start)` and broke the loop to cleanly terminate iteration. Removing the `try...except StopIteration` block causes `StopIteration` raised inside `func` to propagate as an unhandled exception instead of terminating the generator cleanly.
findings_before_overseer.suggested_fix: Keep the `try...except StopIteration: break` handling around `func(start)` so callers can terminate the iteration by raising `StopIteration` from `func`.

stages.name: overseer
trigger_reasons: 1 major/blocker finding(s) from the primary reviewer
stages.notes: F1 is correct. To make it stronger, point out that PEP 479 turns the escaped StopIteration into a RuntimeError rather than letting it bubble up unchanged. Also note that no test covers this case, which is why Layer 1 pytest passed.

findings.summary: `product_index` raises `TypeError` when `element` is a non-sized iterable (e.g., generator or iterator)
findings.evidence: In more_itertools/more.py:4319, `element` is documented and type-hinted as an `Iterable` (e.g. `product_index(element: Iterable[_T], *args: Iterable[_T])`). At line 4332, `elements = tuple(element)` correctly converts the input iterable to a tuple. However, line 4334 was changed from `if len(elements) != len(pools):` to `if len(element) != len(args):`. Passing an iterator or generator (such as a generator expression or `iter(...)`) for `element` raises `TypeError: object of type 'generator' has no len()` before `product_index` can process it.
findings.suggested_fix: Revert the check to `if len(elements) != len(pools):` (or `len(elements) != len(args)`).
